中文

Library code keeps needing one layer of work that is easy to get wrong: timeouts, cancellation, retries, concurrency limits, initialization that runs only once, errors you can recognize, updating deep fields without mutating, and protecting config handed in by callers. `@migaia/utils` handles the edge cases of that layer and gives every kind of failure a stable error code. It has no runtime dependencies and uses no browser-only or Node-only APIs, so it runs in browsers, Node, Bun, Deno and Workers; each group of tools lives under its own subpath for import on demand.

items: The request keeps running after the timeout: with `Promise.race` and `setTimeout`, the caller gets an error on time, yet the request, its connection and the timer are all still alive. The cause: the timeout only ends the waiting and never tells the operation to stop.

Retries make things worse: errors such as 404 are retried too, retries fire immediately, there is no total limit, and the user sees the failure half a minute later. The cause: the retry loop does not tell error kinds apart and has no backoff or overall deadline.

Hundreds of requests go out at once: `Promise.all(ids.map(download))` makes the server start throttling, and queued requests keep running after the user leaves the page. The cause: no concurrency cap and no way to cancel tasks that are still queued.

Initialization runs several times: three modules call a lazy loader at the same moment and open three database connections. The cause: when `if (!db)` runs, the Promise of the first call has not been stored yet.

After a few layers of wrapping, nobody can tell the cause: the only way to check "was it a lost connection" is to compare message text, which breaks as soon as the wording changes. The cause: errors have no stable code, or wrapping dropped the original error.

A timeout really stops the operation instead of only letting the caller return early. With `Promise.race` and `setTimeout` the request keeps running after the timeout; `withTimeout` aborts the operation's `signal` at the deadline before rejecting with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, and `fetch` stops at once. Example

A failure that arrives after the deadline does not disappear. A hand-written `Promise.race` silently swallows it; here it goes to the `report` callback without changing the caller's result, and a rejection with `signal.reason` counts only as acknowledging the cancellation, so it is not misreported. Example

Retries depend on the kind of error and have a total limit. A common retry loop retries even 404s and has no overall time cap; `retry` picks retryable errors with `shouldRetry`, backs off with `delay`, caps the whole run including waits with `totalTimeoutMs`, and throws errors that should not be retried unchanged and at once. Example

A concurrent initialization runs only once. An `if (!db)` lazy loader opens several connections when calls arrive together; `onceAsync` stores the Promise on the first call and every later call gets the same one. Example

Errors stay recognizable by code through any number of wrappers, and the original error keeps its type. Telling causes apart by message text breaks as soon as the wording changes; `attachErrorIdentity` only adds `source` and `code` to the original error, `walkErrorCauses` finds it again along `cause`, and `instanceof` and the stack are preserved. Example

blocks.text: The `signal` that `retry` hands to each request is aborted when its 300 ms are up, and `fetch` stops that request at once instead of waiting in the background. The timeout error is a `UtilsTimeoutError`, which `isUtilsTimeoutError` recognizes; `status` is a field the example adds to its own errors.

Next: to give a single operation a time limit, see `withTimeout`; to cap how many tasks run at once, see `createConcurrencyLimiter`. More runnable scenarios are in Find by scenario in the usage guide.
Here is a common hand-written timeout. It runs, but it has three traps (for illustration only; no need to run it):

`withTimeout` hands the operation a `signal`, and at the deadline it aborts that signal before rejecting; when the operation finishes first, it clears the timer; a failure that arrives after the deadline goes to the `report` callback instead of disappearing. An operation that rejects with the `signal.reason` it received (as `fetch(url, { signal })` does) is only acknowledging the cancellation and is not treated as a new failure.

blocks.text: A few terms used across the module:

items: Cooperative cancellation: a cancellation is only a notice. The operation stops itself once it sees `signal.aborted` or receives the `abort` event on the `signal`; code that never checks the `signal` is not interrupted by force.
Late failure: the operation fails after the result is already settled, for example after the timeout. It goes to `report` and never changes the result the caller already received.
Monotonic clock: `scheduler.now()` comes from `performance.now()` and is used only for intervals and deadlines, not as a date timestamp; use `systemWallClock.timestamp()` when you need a timestamp.
Config ownership: the config `ownConfig` returns belongs to the library, so later edits to the caller's own object cannot reach it.

sections.heading: /promise: when work starts and when a Promise is shared

blocks.text: Prefer the native `Promise.withResolvers()` API when you need to settle a Promise from outside. `deferred()` serves older runtimes that lack it, or project boundaries already expressed through `IDeferred`.
`toPromise(run)` calls `run` immediately in the current call stack and turns its return value or thrown error into a Promise result. If `run` returns a native Promise, the same Promise is returned.

`Promise.resolve().then(run)` waits until the next microtask and returns a new chained Promise. Use `toPromise` when synchronous side effects must happen before the call returns, and `.then(run)` to defer work deliberately; both express failures through rejection.

sections.heading: /scheduler: elapsed time and calendar time use different clocks

blocks.text: `systemScheduler` uses `performance.now()`. Its millisecond `now()` readings never decrease: a later reading can equal an earlier one, but cannot be smaller. They are not Unix timestamps.
With an injected scheduler, calculate deadlines with `scheduler.now()` and schedule their tasks with the same `scheduler.schedule()` so that both use one time base.
`systemWallClock.timestamp()` returns `Date.now()` for dates in logs. Do not subtract it from `now()` or use it in deadline comparisons.

`createManualScheduler()` from `@migaia/utils/testing` is a virtual clock for this repository's tests, rather than an API for external application code. Other projects should prefer their test framework's fake timers; production code uses `systemScheduler` or an injected scheduler that satisfies the same contract.

sections.heading: /error: use codes to decide how to handle a failure

blocks.text: An error's `source` identifies its owner, and `code` identifies the failure within that owner. These are the keys and values of `UtilsErrorCode`. Attaching a code preserves native types such as `TypeError` and `RangeError`; do not depend on message wording.

items: `invalidArgument` / `INVALID_ARGUMENT`: an argument has the wrong type or range; correct it before calling again.
`nonErrorValue` / `NON_ERROR_VALUE`: `toError()` wrapped a thrown value that was not an error; its original value is on `cause`.
`envUnsupported` / `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`: a required host capability is missing; use a suitable host or inject an implementation.
`aborted` / `ABORTED`: an operation observed cooperative cancellation; the original reason remains on the error chain.
`deadlineExceeded` / `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`: an operation, attempt or total deadline expired; inspect `scope` and `timeoutMs` before choosing whether to retry.
`schedulerRunaway` / `SCHEDULER_RUNAWAY`: one virtual-clock advance ran more than 10000 callbacks; check for tasks that keep scheduling work at the same time.
`errorIdentityConflict` / `ERROR_IDENTITY_CONFLICT`: incoming fields conflict with an existing identity; retain the original identity and choose a conflict policy explicitly.
`errorChainInvalid` / `ERROR_CHAIN_INVALID`: a serialized error tree violates its field, depth, count or byte limits; correct the boundary input.
`cloneUnsupported` / `CLONE_UNSUPPORTED`: structured cloning rejected the value; convert it to cloneable data first.
`invalidEncoding` / `INVALID_ENCODING`: encoded bytes or text are malformed; use the reported position to correct the input.
`limiterClosed` / `LIMITER_CLOSED`: a closed concurrency limiter cannot accept new tasks; create a new limiter.
`reentrantCall` / `REENTRANT_CALL`: a non-reentrant operation was called again while it was running; move the nested call outside that execution.
`configUnsupported` / `CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED`: a config root, field or value is outside the supported domain; supply data accepted by the selected profile.
`configReadonly` / `CONFIG_READONLY`: a caller tried to modify read-only config; derive a new config through a patch or merge.
`configConflict` / `CONFIG_CONFLICT`: config sources, profiles or ownership disagree; reconcile their constraints first.
`configLimitExceeded` / `CONFIG_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`: the config graph exceeded a bound, or a limit option is invalid; reduce the input and check the limits.
`configPathInvalid` / `CONFIG_PATH_INVALID`: a config path or key is malformed or unsafe; correct the path.
`configParseFailed` / `CONFIG_PARSE_FAILED`: `ConfigOwner.from()` received a non-string or invalid JSON; the original parser error stays on `cause`.
`configSourceFailed` / `CONFIG_SOURCE_FAILED`: a source supplied to `ConfigOwner.fromAsync()` failed; its rejection stays on `cause`, and the caller chooses whether to retry or use defaults.
`configValueMissing` / `CONFIG_VALUE_MISSING`: `ConfigOwner.require()` found no value at the path; supply it or use `getOr()` with an explicit fallback.
`configValidationFailed` / `CONFIG_VALIDATION_FAILED`: a validator rejected the next config; the previous one stays committed and the validator error stays on `cause`.
`objectPathInvalid` / `OBJECT_PATH_INVALID`: an object path or one of its segments is invalid; correct the path input.
`formatInvalid` / `FORMAT_INVALID`: template syntax or interpolation is invalid; check the template and its values.
`formatValueMissing` / `FORMAT_VALUE_MISSING`: strict template formatting could not find a placeholder's value; supply that data.
`numberFormatInvalid` / `NUMBER_FORMAT_INVALID`: `Intl.NumberFormat` rejected a locale, currency, option or number; correct the formatting arguments.

sections.heading: /bytes: where bytes live and which part a view sees

blocks.text: An `ArrayBuffer` holds raw contiguous memory; it cannot be read or written by numeric index itself. A `Uint8Array` is a view of that memory as unsigned 8-bit integers, each from 0 to 255.

In `new Uint8Array(buffer, byteOffset, length)`, `byteOffset` selects the starting byte. This constructor does not copy the data, so several views can read and write the same underlying `ArrayBuffer`.

Use `slice()` for an independent copy and `subarray()` for a shared window. Writing through the window changes the original array; writing through the copy does not. `SharedArrayBuffer` shares memory across execution environments and has different concurrency semantics, so it is not an isolated copy of an ordinary buffer.

sections.heading: /object: distinguish missing fields, failed reads and copying policies

blocks.text: The first argument to `probeProperty(value, key)` is the object to read. It can be a plain object, a class instance or another object with readable properties.

A missing field and a failed field read have separate outcomes: `missing` can use a business default, while `failed` requires handling the original error. The successful `value` branch consumes the value that was read. Checking the result does not require reading the field again, so a getter runs only once.

`immutableSnapshot(value)` calls the host's `globalThis.structuredClone()` without passing through a JSON string. It preserves cycles and shared references within the graph and supports native cloneable types such as `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `ArrayBuffer` and TypedArray.

It does not preserve a custom class's prototype methods, getters/setters or property descriptors. No transfer list is supplied, so `ArrayBuffer` contents are copied and the source is not detached, the unusable state that follows an ownership transfer.

The function does not call `Object.freeze()`; the returned object remains mutable. Native `structuredClone(value)` works on the whole graph or fails: one unsupported member rejects the clone. `immutableSnapshot(value)` throws `ENV_UNSUPPORTED` when the host lacks the capability, or `CLONE_UNSUPPORTED` when the value cannot be cloned.

`diagnosticSnapshot(value)` projects plain objects, arrays and cloneable built-in subtrees without first cloning the complete graph. Unsupported functions or instances keep their original references, and `diagnostics` records their locations and reasons.

`structuredDiagnosticSnapshot(value)` tries native `structuredClone` first; when cloning fails or the host lacks it, it falls back to that best-effort copy and retains diagnostics about the degradation. These policies suit logs and similar consumers that accept partial copies.
When `diagnostics` is nonempty, check which parts degraded; do not describe the result as a completely isolated snapshot.

`identitySnapshot` returns the original object; calling it alone has no runtime benefit. It is the zero-copy choice in a configurable snapshot policy, the function that decides how a retained value is copied. Choosing it accepts shared references.

Use it only inside a trusted process for objects whose identity matters, or which cannot be cloned, when shared ownership is acceptable. For isolating outside input, retaining historical state or crossing a boundary, choose `immutableSnapshot` and handle cloning failures.

For path updates, immutable describes how the update is made: `set()` neither deep-copies the whole tree nor calls `Object.freeze()`. An actual value change returns a new root. If `Object.is()` considers the old and new values equal, the original root is returned directly.

sections.heading: /config: accept config, expose reads and derive its successor

blocks.text: `ownConfig` is the boundary for outside config: it copies the input and records independently verifiable ownership. A `WeakMap`, a metadata table that adds no fields to the config, retains its `profile` and `limits`. An ordinary object cannot claim admission by forging a field. The default `data` profile accepts data; `richRuntime` also admits callbacks or factories.

The object returned by `ownConfig` is not frozen; ownership and public read-only access are separate concerns. `readonlyConfig` protects the existing config while reads still access its data, without making another copy.

Callers cannot change any level: mutating methods such as `Map.set()`, `Set.add()` and `Date.setFullYear()` throw as well. Expose this view for reads and use `patchConfig()` to produce the next managed config instead of writing to `view`.

Use `readConfigPath` when a missing path must be distinguished from a value of `undefined`. Patches affect root fields only; calculate a new nested subtree first, then supply it as a whole patch value. A `richRuntime` config carrying functions is runtime config and should not be treated as serializable data.

`combineConfig` merges sources in order, with later sources overriding earlier ones. Records merge recursively by default, and arrays are replaced. The example explicitly chooses array concatenation and shows both inputs, the result and a change record prepared by the caller.
Neither `defaults` nor `override` changes. This `diff` only makes the changes explicit; it is not an extra return value from `combineConfig`.

`once(fn)` remembers the first result of a synchronous initialization, including its first thrown error. Each call to `once(fn)` creates a separate cache. Create and export one wrapper at module scope to share it among consumers of that module instance.
Repeated module instances and separate realms, execution environments with their own globals such as iframes, Workers and Node `vm`, do not share this cache. `once` does not ensure global uniqueness.

Let an application entry point or dependency-injection container own an instance that must be shared within one environment. If the application chooses a global location such as `globalThis[Symbol.for('your-app/runtime')]`, it must also manage versions, disposal and test cleanup.

A `Proxy` can turn the first property access into lazy initialization, but uniqueness still depends on where the instance is stored and how many owners create it. Avoid `once` for initialization that needs retries, resets, hot updates or isolation per request.

`onceAsync` suits startup config that never refreshes, a shared SDK client, or dynamically importing and compiling one WASM module. The first call retains a Promise, and other callers reuse it both while it runs and after it settles.

The first failure stays cached, and there is no reset. Put required retries inside the wrapped initializer. For refreshing, rebuilding after logout or isolating work per tenant or request, use a container with that lifecycle.

If the shared task uses one caller's cancellation signal, that caller's cancellation affects every other waiter too. Each wrapper has its own cache; duplicated module instances, iframes, Workers and Node `vm` do not share it.

`IMaybe<T>` distinguishes `{ some: true, value: T }` from `{ some: false }`, including a present undefined. Root exports `isSome`/`isNone` for narrowing, `unwrapOr(m, fallback)` for a same-domain fallback, `mapMaybe(m, mapper)` for one synchronous mapping of a present value, and `toUndefined(m)` when collapsing absence is intentional. None is reused without calling the mapper; mapper results retain identity and are not awaited. Typed optional values receive no extra runtime validation.

Mapper failures retain existing coded errors. An uncoded mutable native Error receives utils INVALID_ARGUMENT on the same instance, preserving native type and stack. An identity conflict wraps the original on cause; failed identity attachment aggregates the original first and the attachment failure second. Non-Error values follow existing toError/NON_ERROR_VALUE semantics.

Recognize the underlying cause after wrapping

sections.heading: Time out a slow request and actually stop it

blocks.text: A slow request gets a timeout and the caller receives the error on time, but the request keeps running in the background and the server keeps working on a result nobody wants.
A timeout built from `Promise.race` and `setTimeout` only lets the caller return early; connections, timers and memory stay alive, because nothing tells the operation to stop.

`withTimeout` hands your operation a `signal`. At the deadline it aborts that signal first and then rejects with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. Pass the signal to `fetch`, or check it in your own code, and the work really stops.
Output:

blocks.code:
query stopped, reason: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
timed out: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED 100

blocks.text: Prints `query stopped, reason: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` and then `timed out: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED 100`.

The operation is cancelled first and clears its own timer, then the caller receives the timeout error; `signal.reason` is that same error. Rejecting with `signal.reason` only acknowledges the cancellation, so it is not reported again as a failure after the deadline.

sections.heading: Where a failure after the deadline goes

blocks.text: Some operations ignore the `signal`, keep running after the deadline and fail later. Where does that failure go?
A hand-written `Promise.race` either loses that late rejection or turns it into an unhandled rejection; either way nobody learns that the write actually failed.

`withTimeout` has already settled with the timeout and never changes the caller's result; the late failure goes to the `report` callback. Without `report` it is rethrown to the host as an uncaught exception, and Node exits the process by default, so always pass `report` for operations that ignore the signal.
Output:

blocks.code:
caller got: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
failure after the deadline: write failed late-rejection

blocks.text: Prints `caller got: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`, then about 40 ms later `failure after the deadline: write failed late-rejection`.
The caller only sees the timeout; the write failure is not lost and reaches `report` with `phase: 'late-rejection'`.

sections.heading: Retry only what is worth retrying

blocks.text: A server sometimes answers 503 and one retry fixes it, but the retry code hammers an already overloaded service and the user waits half a minute before seeing the failure.
Hand-written retry loops have three traps: they retry errors such as 404 that will never succeed, they retry immediately, and they have no total limit.
`retry` asks `shouldRetry` which errors to retry, waits `delay` between attempts (a function can grow it with each attempt), and `totalTimeoutMs` caps the whole run, waits included.
Output:

blocks.code:
attempt 1
attempt 2
attempt 3
stock: 42

blocks.text: Prints `attempt 1`, `attempt 2`, `attempt 3` and `stock: 42`.
After the two 503 responses it waits 100 ms and then 200 ms, and the third attempt succeeds. Each attempt's `signal` is aborted when the total deadline passes.
An order number does not exist and the API answers 404; retrying five times will never succeed and only makes the user wait.
Common retry loops treat every error alike and throw a new wrapper error once attempts run out, so the caller can no longer read the original `status`.

When `shouldRetry` returns `false`, `retry` stops without waiting and throws that original error to the caller. It is not wrapped and its message is unchanged, so the caller can still read its own `status` field.
Output:

blocks.code: calls: 1 error: order not found

blocks.text: Prints `calls: 1 error: order not found`.
The 404 is not retried, `maxAttempts: 5` is only an upper bound, and the caller receives the very error it threw.

sections.heading: Limit a batch and cancel queued tasks when the user leaves

blocks.text: Downloading hundreds of files at once makes the server throttle or fail, and connections queue up.
`Promise.all(ids.map(download))` starts every request at once; nothing limits how many run at the same moment.
`createConcurrencyLimiter` keeps at most `concurrency` tasks running; the rest wait in submission order and start as earlier ones finish.
Output:

blocks.code:
start 1: 2 running, 3 queued
start 2: 2 running, 3 queued
start 3: 2 running, 2 queued
start 4: 2 running, 1 queued
start 5: 2 running, 0 queued
file 1, file 2, file 3, file 4, file 5

blocks.text: `activeCount` stays at 2 while `pendingCount` drops from 3 to 0, and the last line lists `file 1` to `file 5` in submission order.
The `Promise.all` result keeps submission order, whatever order the tasks finish in.
After the user closes the page, queued downloads still run, fetching data for a page nobody will see.
Hand-written queues usually handle queuing but not withdrawal: once a task is queued, all you can do is wait for it to run.

Pass a `signal` to `run`: a task still waiting in the queue rejects with the abort reason and never starts; a task that already started receives the cancellation on `context.signal` and decides itself whether to stop.
Output:

blocks.code:
thumbnail 1 done
thumbnail 2 cancelled: user left the page
thumbnail 3 cancelled: user left the page

blocks.text: Prints `thumbnail 1 done`, then `cancelled: user left the page` for 2 and 3.
Task 1 had already started before the abort, so it finishes; 2 and 3 were still queued, are cancelled and never start.

sections.heading: Run a concurrent initialization only once

blocks.text: Three modules initialize at the same time and three database connections open.
Lazy loading with `let db` and `if (!db)` breaks in async code: when three calls happen at the same moment, `db` is still empty for all of them.
`onceAsync` stores the Promise on the first call, so every later call, including concurrent ones, gets that same Promise.
Output:

blocks.code:
connecting to the database...
connections: 1 same connection: true
ran select 1

blocks.text: Prints `connecting to the database...` once, then `connections: 1 same connection: true`.
All three callers hold the same object: the initialization ran once.
The config service fails on the first initialization. What happens on later calls?
Expecting `onceAsync` to retry by itself after a failure leads to confusion when the service is back and calls still receive the old failure.

`onceAsync` remembers the Promise of the first call, whether it succeeds or fails; every later call receives that same failure and the function does not run again. When the initialization should retry, put `retry` inside the function you pass to `onceAsync`, or create a fresh `onceAsync` after a failure.
Output:

blocks.code:
call 1: config service unreachable
call 2: config service unreachable
call 3: config service unreachable
actual runs: 1

blocks.text: All three calls print `config service unreachable`, and the last line is `actual runs: 1`.
The failure also happens once and is remembered; whether to retry is up to the function you pass in.

sections.heading: Update a deep field without mutating

blocks.text: Changing the city in a user's address does not refresh UI that relies on reference checks, and the original state object was modified too.

Hand-written immutable updates spread every level: `{ ...state, user: { ...state.user, address: { ...state.user.address, city } } }`. With enough levels one gets missed and the original object is mutated.
`set` copies each level along the path and reuses every other branch, leaving the original untouched. `get` reads a path and returns `undefined` when a level is missing instead of throwing.
Output:

blocks.code:
Hangzhou
Shanghai
cart is the same object: true
user is a new object: true
undefined

blocks.text: Prints `Hangzhou` and `Shanghai`: the new object changed and the original did not.
`cart is the same object: true` and `user is a new object: true` show that only objects on the path are copied; the last `undefined` comes from a missing path.

sections.heading: Stop callers from changing config after handing it over

blocks.text: A library's retry count changes mysteriously, and the cause turns out to be a caller editing its own object after handing it over as config.
A library that keeps the caller's config object changes behavior when the caller later edits it, and a plugin that tweaks a field affects everyone else as well.

`ownConfig` copies the config once into an object the library owns; `readonlyConfig` gives plugins a read-only view; `patchConfig` creates a new config instead of changing the old one, and `CONFIG_DELETE` removes a field.
Output:

blocks.code:
attempts seen by the library: 3
read-only view refused the write: TypeError CONFIG_READONLY
https://staging.example.com | debug present: false | retry reused: true

blocks.text: `attempts seen by the library: 3`: the caller's edit did not reach the library.
Writing to the read-only view throws a `TypeError` with code `CONFIG_READONLY`. The new config has the new `endpoint`, no `debug`, and shares the unchanged `retry` object with the old config.

sections.heading: Recognize the underlying cause after wrapping

blocks.text: A lost-connection error is wrapped layer by layer into "failed to load the order", and the upper layer can only compare message text to tell whether the connection was lost.
Comparing messages is fragile: the check breaks as soon as the wording changes, and replacing the error object loses its type and stack.

`attachErrorIdentity` writes a stable `source` and `code` onto the original error without replacing it, so `instanceof` and the stack stay intact; `walkErrorCauses` finds it again along `cause` and `AggregateError.errors`.
Output:

blocks.code:
failed to load the order | lost connection underneath: true
original is still an Error: true

blocks.text: Prints `failed to load the order | lost connection underneath: true`: the outer message is domain text, and the check relies on the code.
`original is still an Error: true`: attaching identity did not change the original error's type.
