blocks.text: Deadlines, cooperative cancellation, retries and concurrency limits. Every cancellation here is cooperative: an aborted operation stops only when it reads the `signal` it was given and returns or throws early on its own; I/O that ignores the `signal` is not interrupted.

The scheduler contract and its implementations are exported only from `@migaia/utils/scheduler` (and the root entry `@migaia/utils`). `sleep`, `withTimeout`, `retry` and `createAbortTimeoutSignal` in this module use it as the type and default of their `scheduler` option.

items: `IScheduler`: the only scheduler contract. `now()` is a monotonic, non-decreasing number of milliseconds (two calls in a row may be equal). Use it only for differences and local deadlines, never as an epoch time. The `delayMs` of `schedule()` must be finite and non-negative; the callback runs at most once and never synchronously inside the `schedule()` call.

`IManualScheduler`: adds `advance(ms)`, which moves virtual time forward and runs due callbacks, and `pendingCount`, the number of tasks that have neither fired nor been cancelled. It is for deterministic unit tests.
`IWallClock`: produces diagnostic timestamps only (epoch milliseconds as a safe integer). Never use it for deadlines, expiry or replay windows.

blocks.code:
export const systemScheduler: IScheduler;
export const systemWallClock: IWallClock;

blocks.text: `systemScheduler` uses `performance.now()` as its monotonic clock and the host `setTimeout` / `clearTimeout` for timers, reading those capabilities through `globalThis` on every call. When the host has no `performance.now`, it returns a non-finite value, or the timer functions are missing, it throws a native error with `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`; an error thrown by `performance.now` itself propagates unchanged. A `delayMs` that is not a number throws `TypeError`, and a non-finite or negative one throws `RangeError`; both carry `INVALID_ARGUMENT` and create no timer. Delays above `2_147_483_647` are waited out in segments; `unref()` uses the native timer as its receiver and keeps applying to later segments; `cancel()` is idempotent.

`systemWallClock.timestamp()` returns `Date.now()`. Use it when you need an epoch timestamp. Code that accepts an `IScheduler` for timeouts, retries or scheduling must pair `scheduler.now()` with `scheduler.schedule()`; never subtract or compare wall-clock values with `now()`.

blocks.code: function createManualScheduler(): IManualScheduler;

blocks.text: For this repository's tests only: it serves unit tests and adapter checks in this repository and is not meant for application code. Other projects should prefer the fake timers of their test framework; production code uses `systemScheduler` or the default scheduler.

Creates a first-in-first-out virtual-clock scheduler: `schedule()` orders tasks by due time, then by registration order. `advance(ms)` runs every due callback in one go; tasks that callbacks schedule along the way also run in the same `advance` as long as they are due at or before the target time. One `advance` that loops more than 10000 times throws `RangeError` / `SCHEDULER_RUNAWAY`, which stops callbacks that keep scheduling each other forever. `delayMs` / `ms` must be finite and non-negative (a non-number throws `TypeError`, anything else invalid throws `RangeError`); a due time or target time that overflows to a non-finite value also throws `RangeError`. All of these carry `INVALID_ARGUMENT` and leave the clock and queue unchanged. Calling `advance()` again inside a callback throws `TypeError` / `REENTRANT_CALL`, and the outer `advance` still completes.
Creates a native Promise that you settle from outside. It helps turn a callback API into a Promise, or lets a test decide exactly when an async operation finishes or fails.
New code should prefer the platform's `Promise.withResolvers()`. `deferred()` mainly serves older runtimes that lack it, or project boundaries that must depend on the `IDeferred<T>` type:

blocks.code:
const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers<number>();
resolve(42);

blocks.text: For older runtimes:

blocks.code: function toPromise<T>(run: () => T): Promise<Awaited<T>>;

blocks.text: Calls `run` synchronously, exactly once, and adopts its return value with native Promise rules. If `run` throws synchronously, the call site does not throw; it returns a Promise rejected with that exact reason. It only turns a synchronous computation into a Promise and creates no timer, scheduler, retry or cancellation state.
Compared with `Promise.resolve().then(() => run())`:

items: `toPromise(run)` calls `run` immediately, so reads, writes and other synchronous side effects have happened before it returns. When `run` returns a native Promise, the result is that same Promise.

`Promise.resolve().then(run)` delays the call to the next microtask and returns a new chained Promise. It is useful for yielding the current call stack or avoiding synchronous reentrancy, not for logic that relies on "takes effect as soon as it is called".
Both turn an exception into a rejection, at different times: the first catches the synchronous exception during the current call, the second only when the microtask actually runs `run`.

blocks.text: Use `toPromise` when work must start synchronously but always return a Promise; use `Promise.resolve().then(run)` when work should start later.

blocks.code: function sleep(delayMs: number, options?: IAsyncControls): Promise<void>;

blocks.text: Resolves after the scheduler delay. If the given `signal` / `signals` abort while waiting, it rejects with `UtilsAbortError`. `delayMs` must be finite and non-negative. It always cleans up its timer and abort listeners; if that cleanup itself throws, the failure goes to `hostRethrowReporter` (`sleep` takes no custom reporter) instead of being swallowed.

`signal` and `signals` are mutually exclusive; passing both rejects with a `TypeError`. `unref: true` tries to call `unref()` on the underlying timer handle, so in Node the timer does not keep the process alive.

Creates one operation signal that several underlying requests can share, without creating, racing or settling any application Promise. When the outside signal aborts first, its original reason is kept; when the deadline comes first, the signal uses the return value of `timeoutReason()`. An error thrown by that reason factory becomes the signal reason and never escapes from the timer callback. Without `timeoutMs`, the outside signal is passed through as the same object. `dispose()` is idempotent and cancels the timer and removes the listener; cleanup failures go to `report` with `operation: 'abort-timeout-signal'`.

The callbacks of `withTimeout` / `raceWithAbort` can also hand one cooperative signal to several requests, but those functions also own the final Promise: its timeout or abort rejection, late rejections and cleanup errors. When a transaction commit is the only fact that settles the work, use this signal-only primitive and let the adapter decide when its Promise completes.

`INativeAbortSignal` is the type of the signal this module creates with a native `AbortController` and hands to the operation. It resolves against the consumer's own global types: with `lib.dom`, `@types/node`, Deno or Bun types it is the host `AbortSignal`, so `fetch(url, { signal })` works directly; without host types it falls back to the structural `IAbortSignal`, so the published declarations need no host library. Every input still accepts the structural `IAbortSignal`.

Wraps a lazy operation in a deadline. The `signal` the `operation` receives is an internal merged signal: it becomes `aborted` when an outside `signal(s)` aborts or when the deadline passes. The operation must check it itself to stop early.

items: `timeoutMs`: must be finite and non-negative. With `timeoutMs === 0` the call rejects at once with `UtilsTimeoutError('operation', 0)` by default; with `zeroTimeoutBehavior: 'start'` it starts the operation immediately and keeps a zero-delay deadline, so an operation that has not settled before the deadline callback still times out.

`cooperativeCancellation` (default `true`): with `false`, no internal `AbortController` is allocated and the operation only receives an inert, never-aborting structural signal (typed `IAbortSignal`, so it cannot go to `fetch`). Use it for "wait at most this long for the result, but the operation does not need to be told to stop".

`report`: once the call has settled, a late success value is discarded and only a late rejection goes to `report` (default `hostRethrowReporter`). When the operation rejects with the exact `signal.reason` it received (as `fetch(url, { signal })` does after it is cancelled), it is only acknowledging the cancellation and nothing goes to `report`. Cleanup failures surface through the returned Promise's rejection or aggregate, not through this reporter.
When cleanup (cancelling the timer, removing listeners) fails, the cleanup errors and the original error are rejected together as an `AggregateError`.

blocks.text: Same semantics as `withTimeout`, but without a deadline timer: the operation fails early only when an outside `signal(s)` aborts. `cleanupPolicy: 'report'` (default `'reject'`) reports a listener cleanup failure as a diagnostic instead of rejecting the final Promise.
Serial retries with three layers of limits:

items: `maxAttempts`: a positive safe integer. If attempt number `maxAttempts` still fails, its error is thrown.
`attemptTimeoutMs`: a separate timeout for each attempt (wrapped in `withTimeout` internally).
`totalTimeoutMs`: a deadline for the whole run, all attempts and backoff waits included; exceeding it throws `UtilsTimeoutError('total', totalTimeoutMs)`.
`shouldRetry(error, context)`: decides whether a failure is worth retrying. Returning `false`, or running out of `maxAttempts`, ends the run and throws that error.

`delay`: a fixed number of milliseconds or a `(error, context) => milliseconds` backoff function for the wait between attempts (done with an internal `sleep`, which also honours `signal` / `signals`).
When an outside signal aborts at any point, the whole run ends with `UtilsAbortError` and no further attempt starts.

blocks.text: `hostRethrowReporter` is the default diagnostic reporter: it rethrows the error with `queueMicrotask` (or synchronously where `queueMicrotask` is missing), so it becomes an uncaught exception that the host's global error handling records instead of being silently swallowed. Replace it through the `report` option with logging, telemetry or similar. In Node an uncaught exception exits the process by default, so pass your own `report` when an operation ignores the `signal` and may fail after the deadline. A rejection with the `signal.reason` the operation received is an acknowledgement of the cancellation, and `withTimeout`, `raceWithAbort` and `retry` never report it.
The only primitive in this module with a lifetime across calls: a first-in-first-out task queue with a concurrency cap.

items: `run(task, { signal })`: adds the task to the queue. Tasks start immediately until `concurrency` is reached; after that they wait for a free slot. Aborting the given `signal` rejects a queued task at once with the abort reason; a task that has already started is not affected and must read `context.signal` itself.
`activeCount` / `pendingCount`: how many tasks are running / waiting in the queue (not cancelled).
`whenIdle()`: a Promise that resolves when no task is running and the queue is empty. Repeated calls share the same wait instead of registering again.
`close(reason?)`: stops accepting new and queued tasks. Queued tasks that have not started reject at once with `reason` (by default a `LIMITER_CLOSED` error); running tasks are not affected.
`dispose(reason?)`: calls `close()` and returns a Promise that resolves only after every running task has finished, for graceful shutdown.

blocks.text: `concurrency` must be a positive safe integer; otherwise the constructor throws `RangeError`.
One set of tools for error identity, wrapping and walking cause chains.

Reads one property exactly once and keeps the getter's receiver. When the read throws, the original thrown value goes into `error`; it is not wrapped and not reported. The caller checks the target object and decides what a failure means. New code that needs a guarded read of a single property should reuse this primitive.
The reason of an outside abort signal is read through the same entry:
Whether a failure is rethrown, wrapped, reported or used as the abort reason depends on the caller's own contract; this primitive only returns the read result.

`UtilsError` is the abstract base class: every semantic error this module throws carries `source: '@migaia/utils'` and a stable `code`. `UtilsAbortError` keeps the original abort reason on `cause`; `UtilsTimeoutError` also carries `scope` (whether the single operation, one attempt or the total deadline ran out) and `timeoutMs`.

Adds non-writable identity fields (`source` / `code` / `phase` / `detail`) to an existing error object in place. It does not replace or wrap the error. If a field already exists with a different value, it throws `TypeError` so it never silently overwrites identity written by other code; the same value counts as idempotent and the error is returned unchanged.

blocks.code: function toError(value: unknown, options?: { readonly message?: string }): Error;

blocks.text: Turns any thrown value into an error you can diagnose. A native `Error`, or a cross-realm / structured error shape with string `name`, `message` and `stack`, is returned as is; the latter is not guaranteed to be `instanceof` the local `Error`. Any other value is wrapped in an internal error type with `cause: value`. Its message is `options.message` when given, otherwise the thrown value itself when it is a string, otherwise a fixed fallback text.

Walks the `cause` chain and `AggregateError.errors` and returns every node visited, starting with `error` itself. A `Set` deduplicates identical values so cycles end. `maxDepth` (default 32) limits the depth; past it, that branch is not followed further. An error created with `cause: undefined` contributes an `undefined` entry, so read fields with optional chaining (`item?.code`).

blocks.code: function combineErrors(errors: Iterable<unknown>, message: string): Error | undefined;

blocks.text: Combines zero, one or many errors: zero gives `undefined`; one is returned as is (normalized with `toError`); several are wrapped in `AggregateError(errors, message)`. If iterating `errors` itself throws, the errors collected so far and that iteration failure are packed into an `AggregateError` and thrown.

Diagnostic shape guards: they check an error-like `name` / `message` / `stack`, `source` equal to `@migaia/utils`, and a `code` that belongs to `UtilsErrorCode`; the abort and timeout guards also check the matching code. They need no `instanceof` against local constructors and are not meant to authenticate where an error came from.

blocks.code:
const UtilsErrorCode = {
  invalidArgument: 'INVALID_ARGUMENT',
  nonErrorValue: 'NON_ERROR_VALUE',
  envUnsupported: 'ENV_UNSUPPORTED',
  aborted: 'ABORTED',
  deadlineExceeded: 'DEADLINE_EXCEEDED',
  schedulerRunaway: 'SCHEDULER_RUNAWAY',
  errorIdentityConflict: 'ERROR_IDENTITY_CONFLICT',
  errorChainInvalid: 'ERROR_CHAIN_INVALID',
  cloneUnsupported: 'CLONE_UNSUPPORTED',
  invalidEncoding: 'INVALID_ENCODING',
  limiterClosed: 'LIMITER_CLOSED',
  reentrantCall: 'REENTRANT_CALL',
  configUnsupported: 'CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED',
  configReadonly: 'CONFIG_READONLY',
  configConflict: 'CONFIG_CONFLICT',
  configLimitExceeded: 'CONFIG_LIMIT_EXCEEDED',
  configPathInvalid: 'CONFIG_PATH_INVALID',
  objectPathInvalid: 'OBJECT_PATH_INVALID',
  formatInvalid: 'FORMAT_INVALID',
  formatValueMissing: 'FORMAT_VALUE_MISSING',
  numberFormatInvalid: 'NUMBER_FORMAT_INVALID'
} as const;

blocks.text: The stable semantic codes used across the whole module; `IUtilsErrorCode` is the union of their values. Besides the `UtilsError` subclasses, native `TypeError` / `RangeError` thrown by modules such as `base64ToBytes`, object paths and config also get the matching `code` (and `source: '@migaia/utils'`) through `Object.defineProperty`, so the same checks recognize them.
What each code means:

items: `INVALID_ARGUMENT`: an argument has the wrong type or range, or a forbidden combination; fix the call.
`NON_ERROR_VALUE`: `toError()` converted a thrown value that was not an `Error`; read the original value from `cause`.
`ENV_UNSUPPORTED`: the host lacks a required capability such as `structuredClone`; switch environment or implementation.
`ABORTED`: an outside signal asked for cancellation; stop the cooperative work and pass the cancellation reason on.
`DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`: an operation, an attempt or the whole run timed out; use `scope` and `timeoutMs` to choose between retrying and degrading.
`SCHEDULER_RUNAWAY`: one advance of the virtual clock ran more than 10000 tasks; look for callbacks that keep scheduling each other at the same instant.
`ERROR_IDENTITY_CONFLICT`: the error already has a different `source` / `code` from the one being attached; keep the original identity.
`ERROR_CHAIN_INVALID`: a received serialized error tree or its plain data breaks the field, scalar, depth, count or text-byte limits; fix the input or use the boundary's own handling policy.
`CLONE_UNSUPPORTED`: `structuredClone` cannot copy the value; convert it to cloneable data first.
`INVALID_ENCODING`: encoded input is not in canonical form; fix the input at the reported offset.
`LIMITER_CLOSED`: the concurrency limiter is closed; stop submitting or create a new one.
`REENTRANT_CALL`: a forbidden reentrant call into the same instance; wait for the current callback to finish.
`CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED`: the config contains an unsupported data shape or property; use plain data.
`CONFIG_READONLY`: an attempt to change a read-only config; create a new config from the owner side.
`CONFIG_CONFLICT`: config sources disagree on ownership, profile or descriptors; align their contracts before merging.
`CONFIG_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`: config key count, depth or a similar safety limit was exceeded; shrink the input or set an explicit limit.
`CONFIG_PATH_INVALID`: a config path is empty, dangerous or has an invalid segment; use a safe path.
`OBJECT_PATH_INVALID`: an object path cannot be parsed safely; fix the string or the segment tuple.
`FORMAT_INVALID`: a template, placeholder or value cannot be formatted safely; fix the template or input.
`FORMAT_VALUE_MISSING`: strict formatting found no value for a placeholder; add the field or change the policy.
`NUMBER_FORMAT_INVALID`: `Intl.NumberFormat` rejected the locale, options, currency or value; fix the format settings.

blocks.text: Byte and text encoding without Node `Buffer` or the DOM, in plain ECMAScript.

items: `ArrayBuffer` is a fixed-length block of raw contiguous memory that only stores bytes; you cannot index into it directly. It is common at `fetch(...).arrayBuffer()`, files, Web Crypto, WebAssembly and Worker transfer boundaries.

`Uint8Array` is an 8-bit unsigned integer view over that memory; each element is one byte from 0 to 255. Base64, UTF-8, network protocols and binary serialization work byte by byte, so this module uses it as its main input and output.

`new Uint8Array(buffer, byteOffset, length)` creates a window that shares the underlying memory and copies nothing; writes through the view show up in the original buffer. `subarray()` keeps sharing memory; only `slice()` makes an independent copy.

A plain `ArrayBuffer` may become detached after it is transferred to a Worker. `SharedArrayBuffer` is memory shared between threads, with different ownership and synchronization rules, so `isArrayBuffer()` rejects it explicitly.

blocks.code:
function isUint8Array(value: unknown): value is Uint8Array;
function isArrayBuffer(value: unknown): value is ArrayBuffer;

blocks.text: Both guards determine the real brand through the engine's `%TypedArray%.prototype[Symbol.toStringTag]` and the internal-slot getter `ArrayBuffer.prototype.byteLength`. They recognize valid instances and subclasses from other iframe / Worker realms, and reject forged `constructor.name`, prototypes or `Symbol.toStringTag`, other TypedArrays, `DataView`, `SharedArrayBuffer` and Proxy objects. The check reads no user properties of the candidate.

A detached `Uint8Array` / `ArrayBuffer` still returns `true`: detaching does not change the object's brand, but it does affect whether bytes can be read, so callers that consume bytes must handle the detached state separately.

blocks.code: function bytesToBase64(value: Uint8Array): string;

blocks.text: Encodes to standard (not URL-safe) Base64 with `=` padding, using the canonical RFC 4648 alphabet.

blocks.code: function base64ToBytes(value: string, target?: Uint8Array): Uint8Array; // target must be exactly the decoded length; it is reused instead of allocating

blocks.text: Only canonical input is accepted: the standard alphabet, a length that is a multiple of 4 and correct `=` padding. Anything else (URL-safe variants, missing padding, stray whitespace and so on) is rejected with a `TypeError` carrying `code: 'INVALID_ENCODING'`. Decoding checks directly that the unused padding bits are zero, without re-encoding, and rejects input whose bits do not line up.

blocks.code:
bytesToBase64(new Uint8Array([1, 2, 3])); // 'AQID'
base64ToBytes('AQID'); // Uint8Array [1, 2, 3]
base64ToBytes('AQID-_'); // throws TypeError (URL-safe characters are not accepted)
function* streamBase64Chunks(value: Uint8Array, maxChunkBytes?: number): Iterable<string>;

blocks.text: Splits a large byte array into Base64 chunks that are each valid on their own: every chunk is cut on a 3-byte boundary, so each one decodes correctly without being joined first. `maxChunkBytes` defaults to `32763` and must be a safe integer `>= 3`; the actual chunk width is rounded down to a multiple of 3.

blocks.code: function utf8ByteLength(value: string): number;

blocks.text: Counts the bytes of a string encoded as UTF-8 without allocating a buffer. Surrogate pairs are handled correctly, and a lone surrogate counts as 3 bytes, the width of U+FFFD.

blocks.code:
function encodeUtf8(value: string): Uint8Array;
function decodeUtf8(value: Uint8Array, options?: { readonly fatal?: boolean }): string;

blocks.text: `encodeUtf8` encodes into a newly allocated UTF-8 byte array. `decodeUtf8` decodes: with `fatal: false` (the default) an invalid byte sequence becomes U+FFFD and decoding skips one byte and continues; with `fatal: true` it throws an encoding error that includes the byte offset (code `INVALID_ENCODING`; the message names UTF-8 and the offset).

blocks.code: function splitUtf8(value: string, maxBytes: number): readonly string[];

blocks.text: Splits a string on code point boundaries so that each piece encodes to at most `maxBytes` bytes; it never cuts a code point in half. `maxBytes` must be a safe integer `>= 4` (4 is the largest UTF-8 width of one code point). An empty string returns `['']`.

blocks.code: splitUtf8('你好世界', 6); // each Chinese character is 3 bytes → ['你好', '世界']

blocks.text: `createSafeRecord<T>()` creates a new null-prototype dictionary on every call and returns `Partial<Record<string, T>>`. Untrusted key names, including `__proto__` and `constructor`, are stored as ordinary data keys and never invoke a setter on `Object.prototype`; after assignment each field is a writable, enumerable, configurable data property. It does not read or copy any input and does not decide key formats for other module.

blocks.code: function isPlainObject(value: unknown): value is Record<PropertyKey, unknown>;

blocks.text: Returns true for a non-array object whose prototype is `null`, or whose prototype's own prototype is `null`. So it also accepts `Object.create(Object.create(null))` rather than only comparing with this realm's `Object.prototype`; ordinary class instances and built-ins such as `Date` / `Map` return false. If reading the prototype chain fails (a proxy trap throws), it also returns `false` instead of throwing.

Reads one property exactly once, so a getter with side effects is not called twice: a missing property gives `missing`; a read (including a getter) that throws gives `failed` with the original error; otherwise it gives `value`.

The first argument can be a plain object, a class instance or any other object with readable properties; the second accepts a string, number or Symbol key. Missing fields and failed reads are separate branches, so a `try/catch` cannot accidentally fall back to a default value; with `failed`, the error is not rebuilt, and `error` is exactly the instance the getter threw.

blocks.code: function immutableSnapshot<T>(value: T): T;

blocks.text: Calls the host's native `globalThis.structuredClone(value)` directly, not JSON serialization or a hand-written recursion. It copies the whole object graph at once and keeps cycles, shared references and the data types structured clone supports, such as `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, `ArrayBuffer` and TypedArrays. This API takes no transfer list, so an `ArrayBuffer` is copied, never transferred.

Structured clone does not keep custom class prototype methods, getters / setters or property descriptors; functions, `WeakMap` and other unsupported members make the whole clone fail. "Immutable" means the snapshot no longer shares references with the source, not that the result went through `Object.freeze()`; freeze it or make it read-only yourself when you need that at runtime. A host without `structuredClone` throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'ENV_UNSUPPORTED'`; a value that cannot be cloned throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'CLONE_UNSUPPORTED'`.

The key difference from native `structuredClone` / `immutableSnapshot` is how failure is handled: those two are all-or-nothing for the whole graph, and any unsupported member makes the call throw; `diagnosticSnapshot` always tries to return `{ value, diagnostics }`. It copies plain objects and arrays recursively and calls `structuredClone` separately on each cloneable built-in subtree; functions, class instances and other unsupported types keep their original reference and are recorded as `unsupported`. An accessor is read once, turned into a plain value and recorded as `accessor`; a failed read or reflection is recorded as `read-failed`. A `WeakMap` keeps cycles safe.

So the result of `diagnosticSnapshot` may be only partly isolated: when `diagnostics` is not empty, the caller must check the listed `path`s and must not treat the result as a full deep copy. It suits logs, telemetry and debugging panels, where the data must not be lost wholesale but any degradation must be visible; security boundaries and config isolation should still use `immutableSnapshot` and let failures stop explicitly.

`structuredDiagnosticSnapshot` combines the two strategies: it first tries native `structuredClone`, and on success `diagnostics` is empty; if the host lacks it or the clone fails, it falls back to the best-effort snapshot above and adds an `unsupported` diagnostic, or a `read-failed` one carrying the original cause, at the root path. Prefer it at telemetry boundaries that want "a full clone when possible, otherwise an observable degraded result".

blocks.code: function identitySnapshot<T>(value: T): T;

blocks.text: Returns its argument unchanged. Called alone it has no runtime benefit; it is the zero-copy branch for configurable strategy slots such as `snapshot` / `clone`, and states explicitly that the caller accepts a shared reference whose later changes both sides will see. This repository's clone policy uses it for its `opaque` branch, which serves trusted in-process data that is identity-sensitive or not cloneable and may be shared. Do not use it where outside input must be isolated, for history snapshots or when crossing a boundary; choose `immutableSnapshot` there.

sections.heading: Object paths (parseObjectPath / probeObjectPath / get / set / createPathAccessor)

blocks.text: Object paths come in two forms:

items: String paths: `a.b.c`, with bracketed indexes for arrays: `list.[0].name`.
Tuple paths: `readonly ['a', 'b', 'c']` or `readonly ['list', 0, 'name']`, which may include `symbol` keys (a string path cannot express a symbol).

blocks.text: Both forms share the same safety limits: at most 512 characters per segment, at most 256 segments, and at most 4096 characters for a whole string path; `__proto__` / `prototype` / `constructor` are always rejected, which prevents prototype pollution.

blocks.code: function parseObjectPath(path: string | IObjectPathTuple): IObjectPathTuple;

blocks.text: Parses a string path into a normalized `readonly` tuple of segments (numeric indexes become `number`), or validates and freezes a given tuple path. Any out-of-range or dangerous segment throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'OBJECT_PATH_INVALID'`.

Probes the path segment by segment, reading each segment once. The four results mean: a value was found (`value`, carrying `value`); a property on the path does not exist (`missing`); a parent value on the path is not an object or function, so the probe cannot go deeper (`blocked`, for example the path is `a.b.c` but `a.b` is `null` or a string); and reading a segment threw (`failed`, for example a throwing getter, carrying `error`).

All four results share `originKey` (the `path` exactly as passed) and `segments` (the full tuple parsed by `parseObjectPath`). `missing` / `blocked` / `failed` also share `failedAt` (the 0-based index of the failing segment), `failedKey` (that segment's key), `resolvedPath` (the prefix that resolved, i.e. the segments before `failedAt`) and `parent` (the parent value at the point of failure: for `missing` / `failed` the object that should own the property, for `blocked` the non-object value itself). Only `failed` adds `error`, the original thrown value.

`probeObjectPathSegments` accepts a tuple the caller has already validated or cached and skips parsing; its results mean exactly the same as `probeObjectPath`. Use it only on hot internal paths that guarantee the segments already passed the same safety rules; send outside string input to `probeObjectPath`.

A simplified read on top of `probeObjectPath`: `missing` / `blocked` both return `undefined`; `failed` (the read itself threw) rethrows that error instead of swallowing it. This differs from "the path does not exist", so callers handle the two separately.

blocks.code:
const data = { user: { name: 'Ada' } };
get(data, 'user.name'); // 'Ada'
get(data, 'user.missing'); // undefined (missing)
get(data, 'user.name.x'); // undefined (blocked: 'Ada' is a string, so .x cannot be reached)

blocks.text: An immutable path write: every `set()` that really changes a value returns a new root object and leaves the input unchanged. Only nodes on the path are shallow-copied (structural sharing: untouched sibling nodes keep the same reference). "Immutable" describes how the update happens; it does not mean the result was deep-copied or frozen, and the returned object can still be modified. Missing containers on the way are created from the type of the next key (a number key creates `[]`, anything else `{}`). If the path runs into a non-empty primitive (a string, number and so on) that cannot be entered, it throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'OBJECT_PATH_INVALID'`. If the new value is `Object.is`-equal to the old one, no update happens and the original object is reused without copying.

blocks.code:
const before = { user: { name: 'Ada', tags: ['a'] } };
const after = set(before, 'user.name', 'Grace');
after.user.name; // 'Grace'
after !== before; // true (an update returns a new root)
after.user !== before.user; // true (nodes on the updated path are copied)
after.user.tags === before.user.tags; // true (untouched branches keep their reference)
before.user.name; // 'Ada' (the original was not modified)
Object.isFrozen(after); // false (an immutable update is not a freeze)

blocks.text: Wraps a stateful accessor that holds the current root internally: after each successful `set()`, `accessor.value` moves to the new root, and later `get` / `set` calls work on the latest root. `ifMissing` / `ifBlocked` / `ifFailed` are called when the matching probe result occurs, as central diagnostic hooks.

`onGet` / `onSet` are called on every successful read / write. Event fields: `originKey` (the path as passed), `segments` (the parsed tuple), `probe` (the `IPathValueProbe` this read / write hit, i.e. the successful probe), `value` (the value actually read / about to be written) and `replace(value)`, which changes the returned value or the written value of this read / write in place, for example to fill defaults or validate and convert before writing. `IPathGetEvent` and `IPathSetEvent` differ only in the type of `value` / `replace`: reads use `IObjectPathValue` (the type read), writes use `IObjectPathWriteValue` (the widened writable type).

The matching type tools, which give callers path completion and value types at compile time: `IObjectPathSegment`, `IObjectPathTuple`, `IObjectPath<T>` (string paths, at most 8 levels deep), `IObjectPathTupleFor<T>` (tuple paths), `IObjectPathInput<T>` (the union of both), `IObjectPathValue<T, P>` (the type the path points to) and `IObjectPathWriteValue<T, P>` (the type accepted when writing; literal types are widened to their base type, for example a union of literals becomes `string` / `number` / `boolean` / `bigint`).

`@migaia/utils/typing` (`src/typing.ts`) is a type-only entry: the file contains only `export type` and no runtime values, and the build output `dist/typing.js` has no executable code. It is not re-exported from the root entry `@migaia/utils`; you can only write `import type { ... } from '@migaia/utils/typing'`. This is deliberate: keeping the type entry apart from runtime entries means referring to these types never pulls runtime code in through module resolution.
It does two things:
1. Re-exports types defined elsewhere, giving cross-module type reuse one stable entry, so consumers do not have to remember whether a type lives in `/object` or `/promise`:

items: From `/object` (that is, `object-path.ts`): `IObjectPath`, `IObjectPathInput`, `IObjectPathSegment`, `IObjectPathTuple`, `IObjectPathTupleFor`, `IObjectPathValue`, `IObjectPathWriteValue`
From `/object` (that is, `object.ts`): `IProbePropertyResult`
From `/promise`: `IAbortSignal`, `IDeferred`

blocks.text: These types mean exactly what their source modules define (two entries for the same type, not two separate definitions); see the `/object` module and `/promise` module sections for full details.
2. Adds two type tools that `/object` does not provide, which turn a discriminated union into a map from discriminant value to the matching union branch:

items: Type parameter `F extends PropertyKey`: the discriminant field name (`string` / `number` / `symbol`).

Type parameter `T extends Record<F, PropertyKey>`: the union itself. The constraint requires the `F` field of every member to be a `PropertyKey`; if a branch's field is an object or another non-`PropertyKey` type, `T` does not satisfy `Record<F, PropertyKey>` and compilation fails (a compile error, not a runtime one: the tool simply cannot be used).
Result: a mapped type keyed by each literal value of `T[F]`, whose value is `Extract<T, Record<F, K>>`, the branch for that discriminant (several branches sharing a value stay a union).
Type parameter `T`: the union itself.

Type parameter `P extends IObjectPathInput<T>`: a string path (such as `'meta.category'`) or a tuple path (such as `readonly ['meta', 'category']`), written exactly as `get` / `set` in `/object` accept them.

The path must resolve on every branch of the union, and the value must narrow to a `PropertyKey`. A branch where the path is missing or has the wrong type is excluded by a conditional type rather than raising a runtime error. This is purely type-level: when some branches lack the path or have a non-`PropertyKey` value, the result may be a map missing those branches, or even an empty object type, and the alias declaration is not guaranteed to fail compilation.
Result: a map keyed by each literal discriminant the path resolves to, whose value is the matching branch (branches sharing a value become a union).

blocks.text: Example (from the module's own test `test/typing.test.ts`, checked with `expectTypeOf`):
Type limits: a path that exists on no branch violates the path constraint; a path missing on some branches, or resolving to a non-`PropertyKey`, may just produce an empty map.

Config objects with ownership: only objects accepted by `ownConfig` can go through `readonlyConfig` / `patchConfig` / `readConfigPath` / `combineConfig`. A runtime `WeakMap` of metadata, not a field that could be forged, marks "this is a config root managed by this module".

blocks.code:
const ConfigProfile = { data: 'data', richRuntime: 'richRuntime' } as const;
type IConfigProfile = 'data' | 'richRuntime';

blocks.text: `data` (the default) accepts only portable plain data: plain objects, arrays and built-ins such as `Date` / `RegExp` / `Map` / `Set`; functions are rejected. `richRuntime` also accepts functions and constructable classes (deep-copied together with their own properties and `prototype`), for configs that really need to carry callbacks or factories.

blocks.code: const CONFIG_DELETE: unique symbol;

blocks.text: In a `patchConfig` / `combineConfig` patch, setting a key to this symbol means "delete this key" rather than "set it to `undefined`".
Deep-copies `value` into an independent graph that this module's metadata marks as "owned". The root must be a plain object (not an array) without `symbol` keys. While copying:

items: `Date` / `RegExp` / `Map` / `Set` are recognized and rebuilt as new instances (instead of being walked as plain objects);
cycles keep the same graph shape through an internal `WeakMap` (no infinite recursion, and shared nodes stay shared);
`__proto__` / `prototype` / `constructor` keys are always rejected;
exceeding the depth / node / key limits in `limits` (below) throws a `RangeError` with `code: 'CONFIG_LIMIT_EXCEEDED'`.

blocks.text: If `value` is already the result of an earlier `ownConfig` with matching metadata (the same `profile` / `limits`), it is returned unchanged (idempotent); if the metadata differs (for example the same object passed with another `profile`), it throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'CONFIG_CONFLICT'`.

With the result in hand, the caller has three clear paths: keep using it internally as a stable config root; expose a readable but not writable recursive Proxy through `readonlyConfig()`; or derive the next owned config through `patchConfig()` or `combineConfig()`. Do not pass the original outside object to these APIs, and do not mistake "owned" for "frozen": the ownership guarantee comes from the independent graph and the internal registration, while runtime write protection comes separately from `readonlyConfig()`.

`limits` may not exceed the module defaults. `patchConfig` may only tighten the limits of its base; widening them throws `CONFIG_CONFLICT`. `combineConfig` takes the field-by-field minimum of all inputs and the requested limits, so a widening request is tightened automatically and does not throw `CONFIG_CONFLICT`.

blocks.code: function readonlyConfig<T extends IConfigRecord>(value: IOwnedConfig<T>): T;

blocks.text: Returns a cached read-only object that intercepts changes with a `Proxy`; calling it again with the same input returns the same read-only object. Reads still go to the original config, and no second copy of the data is made. Every write (`set` / `defineProperty` / `deleteProperty` / `setPrototypeOf` / `preventExtensions`, and mutating methods on `Map` / `Set` / `Date` such as `.set()` / `.add()` / `.setFullYear()`) throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'CONFIG_READONLY'`. Nested objects, `Map`, `Set` and function fields get the same write protection. `value` must come from `ownConfig`, otherwise it throws `code: 'CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED'`.

A copy-on-write overlay at the root: each key in `patch` either gets a new value (deep-copied recursively and brought under ownership) or `CONFIG_DELETE`, which deletes it. Only nodes on changed paths are copied; untouched subtrees are shared by reference. With an empty `patch` and `reuseUnchangedRoot` (default `true`), `base` itself is returned without copying. `patch` must be a plain object without `symbol` keys or accessor properties, otherwise it throws `code: 'CONFIG_UNSUPPORTED'`; a key named `__proto__` / `prototype` / `constructor` throws `code: 'CONFIG_PATH_INVALID'`. Note: `patchConfig` applies the patch at the root only. To change a nested field, compute the new nested subtree in your code with `get` / `set` (`/object`) and put it into `patch` as a whole value.

Builds on `parseObjectPath` from `/object` and adds config-specific limits (customizable lengths, defaulting to the module defaults). Every segment becomes a string: numeric index shorthand is not treated specially in config paths.

Reads one path inside a config and tells "the key does not exist" (`missing`) from "the value is `undefined`" (`value: undefined`). Object or function values are wrapped in the same read-only Proxy as `readonlyConfig`, so nested values read this way cannot be changed from outside either. `config` must come from `ownConfig`.

Merges several owned config roots in the order of `sources` (later ones override earlier ones). With a single source and no merge options, that source is returned and its root identity is kept; every other case produces a new owned config. All sources must share one `profile`, otherwise it throws `code: 'CONFIG_CONFLICT'`.

`strategies` are the global defaults; `pathRules` is a list of `{ prefix, strategies }` matched by `prefix` (a key path from the root) against the key path currently being merged. The rule with the longer (more specific) `prefix` wins, and a matching rule is merged with the global `strategies` (fields the rule declares override the global ones; fields it does not declare keep the global values).

When a key exists on both sides and falls outside every automatic merge case (for example two primitive values that cannot be merged), and `onConflict` is given, it is called with an `IConfigConflictContext` (`path`: the full path of the key; `left`: the existing value; `right`: the new value). Its `IConfigConflictDecision` decides the result: `{ kind: 'left' }` keeps the left value, `{ kind: 'right' }` takes the right value, `{ kind: 'delete' }` deletes the key, and `{ kind: 'value', value }` uses a custom value. `onConflict` must return synchronously: returning a Promise throws `code: 'CONFIG_CONFLICT'`, and so does a return value that is not one of the four kinds. Without `onConflict`, the right side simply overrides the left (standard merge semantics). `right === CONFIG_DELETE` deletes the target key, which lets a merge strip a default written by an earlier source.

blocks.code: const noop: () => undefined;

blocks.text: An empty function that always returns `undefined`, used as a default callback.

blocks.code: function once<T extends (...args: never[]) => unknown>(functionValue: T): T;

blocks.text: Memoizes a synchronous function: it really runs only on the first call, and later calls return the first result directly (or rethrow the first exception; exceptions are cached too, so the body does not run again on the second call). If the wrapped function is called again while the first call is still running (the body calls the wrapped function itself), it throws a `TypeError` with `code: 'REENTRANT_CALL'`, which stops accidental recursion from bypassing the cache.

It suits expensive, deterministic synchronous initialization inside a module, such as building a read-only registry, compiling a schema or detecting a runtime capability once. The first exception is cached forever, so do not use it when you need retry, reset, hot reload or per-request isolation.

Be precise about its scope: every call to `once(fn)` creates a new wrapper with its own cache. Creating and exporting a single wrapper at module top level gives "one per module instance"; but duplicate bundles, iframes, Workers and Node `vm` have separate module instances, so it is not a cross-realm global singleton. When something really must be shared across a realm or process, let the application entry or a dependency-injection container hold the instance; if you must use a global table, you can use `globalThis[Symbol.for('your-app/runtime')]` and handle version conflicts, lifecycle and test cleanup yourself.

A `Proxy` can turn the first property access into lazy initialization or restrict access, but it provides no uniqueness by itself. Whether something is a singleton still depends on where the instance behind the Proxy is stored and how many owners it has, so there is no need to wrap the result of `once` in a Proxy to get a "real singleton".

blocks.code: function onceAsync<T>(functionValue: () => PromiseLike<T>): () => Promise<T>;

blocks.text: Memoizes one asynchronous call: the first call starts `functionValue()`, and the wrapper keeps and returns that same Promise; every later call, whether the Promise is pending, fulfilled or rejected, gets this Promise. `functionValue()` may return a native `Promise` or a valid PromiseLike; any other value makes the shared Promise reject with a `TypeError` carrying `code: 'INVALID_ARGUMENT'`.

It suits async initialization that should run only once in the life of a page or process, such as loading a startup config that never refreshes, initializing a shared SDK client, or importing and compiling the same WASM module. It solves both "do not start twice under concurrency" and "keep reusing the result afterwards".

It does not suit per-key deduplication, periodic refresh, retry after failure, rebuilding after logout, or isolation per tenant or request. The first rejection is cached forever and there is no reset. If the underlying task uses one caller's `AbortSignal`, that caller cancelling the task also affects every waiter on the shared Promise. Use a cache or lifecycle container with an invalidation policy for those needs.

Every call to `onceAsync(fn)` creates its own cache; modules instantiated more than once, or code spread across iframes, Workers or Node `vm`, do not share it, so it is not a cross-realm global task coordinator either.
The Collector is a lazy, array-only query pipeline from the module root entry:
Evaluation and caching:

items: `collect` borrows the original `readonly` array without copying it; with no actions, or when every source passes, `result` reuses the original array.

Each action is written into an ordered pipeline right away but does not scan the source; the first read of `result` walks the source once and caches it. Repeated reads at the same revision return the same reference; adding an effective action invalidates the cache.
Action order is observable: `take(2).where(predicate)` is not the same as `where(predicate).take(2)`. Chained calls create no intermediate arrays per step.

Failed evaluations are not cached; errors thrown by getters, Proxy objects and `where` keep their original identity. Reading or changing the same collector again from inside an evaluation callback throws `REENTRANT_CALL`.

blocks.text: Field actions:

items: `fieldBy` parses its paths immediately and adds a filter "at least one field value is not `undefined`"; missing, blocked and explicit `undefined` all count as no value. Calling it again keeps the earlier filter and replaces the active field set for the field predicates that follow.

`like` runs `trim().toLowerCase()` on the query; an empty query after trimming does nothing. It matches only string fields, as a case-insensitive contiguous substring, and several fields combine with OR.

`equals` and `oneOf` use `Object.is`; several fields combine with OR, and several actions combine in order with AND. `oneOf` always scans its candidates linearly and never upgrades to an index, whatever the data size.
`distinctBy` deduplicates only defined keys and keeps the first occurrence; missing, blocked and explicit `undefined` values take no part in deduplication.
`where` receives only the source item, no index. `skip` / `take` accept only non-negative safe integers and otherwise throw a native `RangeError` with `INVALID_ARGUMENT`.

blocks.text: The caller keeps the input array and nested sources read-only. The Collector does not watch outside changes; after data is changed behind the type system, a cached revision does not invalidate itself.
This combination is for verification in this repository's tests, not an example of production code. Outside tests should prefer their test framework's fake timers.

`createManualScheduler()` makes time deterministic, so unit tests can assert timeout and retry behavior precisely. Timeout cancellation is cooperative: `retry` and application code must read the `signal` they are given to stop early. `ownConfig` copies and registers its input; `readonlyConfig` returns a cached object that can be read but not changed; `patchConfig` returns a new managed config, and `CONFIG_DELETE` only works in root-level patches.

sections.heading: Concurrency limit + retry + combined errors: fetch a batch and tolerate partial failure

blocks.text: `combineErrors` returns `undefined` when nothing failed, the failure itself when exactly one failed, and an `AggregateError` when several failed.

sections.heading: Object paths + config: write a changed nested structure back to the config root
One-time initialization + error identity: give an initialization failure a recognizable code

blocks.text: `once` remembers the first thrown error; every later call throws that same error object and does not initialize again.

blocks.code:
import { detectServerRuntime } from '@migaia/utils'

console.log(detectServerRuntime()) // 'node' in Node

blocks.text: `detectServerRuntime(): 'deno' | 'bun' | 'node' | undefined` checks `globalThis.Deno`, then `process.versions.bun`, then `process.versions.node`. Node compatibility globals in Deno and Bun do not take precedence. Browsers return `undefined`. The function imports no filesystem or other host APIs; native adapters use its result to load only their runtime module.

`jitter(value, ratio, random = Math.random)` is exported from `@migaia/utils/number` and the root entry. It returns a value in `[value * (1 - ratio), value]`, only shortening the deadline. `value` must be finite and non-negative; `ratio` and the random result must be in the inclusive interval `[0, 1]`. Invalid inputs throw a `RangeError` carrying `@migaia/utils` / `INVALID_ARGUMENT`. A throwing random callback produces the same coded error with the original failure on `cause`. Each call with valid arguments draws exactly one sample, including when `value` or `ratio` is zero.

blocks.code:
import { jitter } from '@migaia/utils/number'

console.log(jitter(60_000, 0.2, () => 0.5)) // 54000, never above the original 60000

blocks.text: `isSafeIntegerValue(value)` from `/value` accepts only finite safe-integer numbers and converts no strings, bigints or boxed numbers.

`tryString(value)` from `/string` passes strings through unchanged and runs native `String(value)` exactly once on anything else. It returns `{ threw: false, value: string }` or `{ threw: true, error: unknown }`; a failure keeps the exact thrown value, with no fallback, no reporter call and no new error. The caller decides at its own boundary whether to report, fall back or rethrow:

`isNullish` recognizes only `null | undefined`; `isBlankString` only strings that are empty after `trim`. `isEmptyValue` combines the two and also treats `NaN` as empty; `0`, `0n`, `false`, arrays and objects stay real values. `isPrimitive` covers all seven JavaScript primitive types without creating an extra type tag.

`format(source, values, options?)` replaces `{path}` in one linear scan; nested paths read only own properties, and missing values keep their placeholder by default. `options.placeholder` sets `{ open, close }`, `missing` can be `preserve | empty | throw`, and `nullish` can be `empty | stringify`. Doubling a delimiter character prints it literally.

`formatNumber`, `formatCurrency`, `formatPercent`, `formatInteger` and `formatCompactNumber` share one bounded cache of 64 `Intl.NumberFormat` instances. Hot loops such as tables, market data or inventory should use `createNumberFormatter(options)` so options are not parsed for every item. The caller explicitly owns every locale, currency, precision and rounding rule.

items: A timeout did not interrupt the I/O: expected. Cooperative cancellation requires the operation to read and act on the `signal` it was given; pass the `signal` down to the I/O (for example `fetch(url, { signal })`) so it honours the abort.
`base64ToBytes` rejected the input: have the producer emit standard, padded RFC 4648 text; URL-safe (`-` / `_`) or unpadded variants are not accepted and must be converted to the standard form first.

Writing a read-only config throws: deliberate; `readonlyConfig` exists to prevent accidental changes. To change it, call `patchConfig` on the original owned config instead of modifying the read-only object.

`once` reports a reentrancy error: the body called the same wrapped function again before the first call returned. Move the recursive logic outside the wrapper, or let a plain function recurse on itself.

You need "current value subscription / replay" or a resource release lifecycle: `@migaia/utils` provides no reactive state or resource ownership model; use a dedicated reactive or lifecycle module instead of looking for a substitute here.

`ownConfig` / `patchConfig` throw `CONFIG_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`: the config graph exceeded the depth / node / key limits. Check for unexpected deep nesting or cyclic growth, and tighten `limits` or shrink the data if needed; the module defaults cannot be widened.

blocks.text: Import `isNativeErrorValue(value)` from `@migaia/utils/error` (or the root). It recognizes Error-family prototype chains, helping boundaries keep the original Error identity; it calls no methods on the input, and a proxy it cannot inspect returns false. It is only a diagnostic shape check and must not be used to authenticate untrusted input.

sections.heading: deferTask and the scheduler's optional defer

blocks.text: An `IScheduler` may also provide `defer(callback): void` for jobs that should run "after the current call", which is different from cancellable timers. `deferTask(clock, callback)` uses the scheduler's `defer` when present and falls back to `schedule(callback, 0)` otherwise. The root entry and the `/scheduler` subpath export the same function. `systemScheduler`'s `defer` uses a native microtask and keeps microtask ordering; a custom scheduler decides its own timing. The caller owns any Promise the callback returns; an error thrown while registering keeps its identity. This API creates no new queue and returns no cancellation handle.

A callback or method that is not a function throws a native `TypeError` with `@migaia/utils` / `INVALID_ARGUMENT`; when reading the `defer` method itself fails, the original error is kept on `cause`. With the default `systemScheduler` and no `queueMicrotask` on the host it throws `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`; an explicitly passed manual or host clock does not need that global. Copying `systemScheduler` with spread syntax also copies its `defer`, so override `defer` too when you change how deferred jobs are delivered.
A fatal UTF-8 decoding failure uses `INVALID_ENCODING` and names UTF-8 and the byte offset in its message; Base64 failures still name Base64.

The table lists every public name. See the module sections above for parameters, errors and lifecycle constraints; type tools are listed with their purpose too. The URL helpers only read structure and do not check whether a URL is valid or safe.

blocks.text: `IMaybe<T>` distinguishes `{ some: true, value: T }` from `{ some: false }`, including a present undefined. Root exports `isSome`/`isNone` for narrowing, `unwrapOr(m, fallback)` for a same-domain fallback, `mapMaybe(m, mapper)` for one synchronous mapping of a present value, and `toUndefined(m)` when collapsing absence is intentional. None is reused without calling the mapper; mapper results retain identity and are not awaited. Typed optional values receive no extra runtime validation.

Mapper failures retain existing coded errors. An uncoded mutable native Error receives utils INVALID_ARGUMENT on the same instance, preserving native type and stack. An identity conflict wraps the original on cause; failed identity attachment aggregates the original first and the attachment failure second. Non-Error values follow existing toError/NON_ERROR_VALUE semantics.
English
`@migaia/wasm` 提供对齐的 WASM 字节暂存区，以及同步的 JSON 与 MessagePack 转码；你显式管理字节的所有权，不把 JavaScript 对象图逐字段传过 WASM 边界。MessagePack 是一种二进制数据格式。

items: 创建数值视图时抛出 `RangeError`：字节分配器给出的偏移没有满足 `Float64Array` 或 `BigInt64Array` 的对齐要求。
大分配后旧读数消失：数值视图跨越内存增长被缓存，仍指向已经失效的旧缓冲。
第二次导出覆盖第一次结果：输出元数据放在共享的“上一次结果”中，没有绑定到各自操作。
归档看起来成功，尾部数据却丢失：只解析第一个文档，没有检查剩余的非空白输入。
清理后待上传数据变了：队列保留了已释放 WASM 内存的视图，没有取得 JavaScript 自有副本。
数值视图不需要另写对齐器。 Rust 使用 `Vec<u64>`，分配地址按八字节对齐，容量向上取整；数值读数示例直接建立 `Float64Array`。
交错转码不会串用“上一次结果”。 每次调用返回独立的输出 id、精确长度和错误；交错转码示例保留两个结果后再读取。
拼接损坏会明确失败。 转码器检查单文档边界，不会把第二个文档悄悄丢掉；尾随文档示例得到零输出和当前操作的错误。
输入输出都按字节交付。 JSON 读取器直接写入 MessagePack 输出，不先构造 `serde_json::Value` 树；交错转码示例把 JSON 字节交给转码器，并保留每次操作自己的输出。这里描述机制，不承诺相对原生 JSON 操作的速度。

blocks.text: arena（字节暂存区）是模块内部保存字节的地方。`alloc_bytes(byte_len)` 返回稳定的非零分配 id；内存或 id 空间耗尽时返回 `0`。`ptr_of(id)` 返回字节偏移，`byte_len_of(id)` 返回向上取整为八倍数的容量。未知或已释放 id 的两个查询都返回 `0`。`dealloc_bytes(id)` 返回是否确实移除了活动分配。每次成功分配都必须显式释放，包括零长度分配。

`json_to_msgpack(id, len)` 和 `msgpack_to_json(id, len)` 每次返回独立的 `ConversionResult`。成功时它持有新的输出 `id`、精确输出长度 `len` 和空串 `error`；失败时 `id`、`len` 为零，`error` 解释本次失败。转码不会释放输入。输入和成功输出 id 用 `dealloc_bytes` 释放；成功或失败的结果元数据都要另行调用 `result.free()`。`free()` 不释放输出字节区。

转码只接受一个完整文档。JSON 允许文档后的空白；MessagePack 必须精确消费传入长度。长度必须是有效载荷字节数，不能用取整后的容量。JSON 对象的 map key 保持字符串。JSON 对象直接按 map 序列化，不依赖 struct-map 配置。往返保真限于 JSON 数据模型及可表示数值；任意 MessagePack 的 bin/ext、非 JSON map key 和超出 JSON 数值范围的整数可能被改写或拒绝。

指针只保证释放前稳定，内存增长会替换 `memory.buffer`。每次读取前用当前缓冲重新创建视图。`.slice()` 得到 JavaScript 自有副本，可以在释放字节区后保留；零拷贝视图则要求把对应 id 的释放延后到最后一次读取之后。`@migaia/store-wasm` 额外提供字段所有权和 `FinalizationRegistry` 兜底，但不替代确定性释放，也不复制这里的暂存区。
模块只发布第一份完成初始化的导出。并发调用和具名函数使用同一份内存与暂存区；仍可能并发实例化，不承诺同一个 Promise 或只编译一次。原生 `WebAssembly.CompileError`、`LinkError` 和 `RuntimeError` 原样透传，不附加包级 `source` 或 `code`。转码失败通过返回值报告，与这些原生异常不同。

sections.heading: 内存增长后继续读取同一块分配

blocks.text: 后续分配触发内存增长后，之前缓存的数值视图可能变成空视图。指针稳定不代表旧 ArrayBuffer 仍然有效。保留分配 `id`，每次读取前用 `ptr_of` 和当前 `memory.buffer` 重新创建视图。
输出：

blocks.code:
偏移未变: true
旧视图字节数: 0
当前读数: 42

blocks.text: 输出 `偏移未变: true`、`旧视图字节数: 0` 和 `当前读数: 42`。活动分配的偏移保持不变，但内存增长使旧的非共享缓冲失效。

sections.heading: 释放 WASM 字节后保留 JavaScript 副本

blocks.text: 上传队列可能比产生字节的转码任务活得更久。如果队列还拿着已释放字节区的视图，后续分配就可能改写待上传数据。在 `dealloc_bytes` 前复制字节，队列就拥有独立副本；第二次释放返回 `false`，不会释放另一块活动分配。
输出：

blocks.code:
释放: true false
副本: 1,2,3
已释放的查询: 0 0

blocks.text: 输出 `释放: true false`、`副本: 1,2,3` 和 `已释放的查询: 0 0`。JavaScript 副本仍可读取，已释放 id 的字节区查询返回零。

sections.id: 保留两次转码结果而不互相覆盖
sections.heading: 保留两次转码结果而不互相覆盖

blocks.text: 批量导出可能还没读取第一次结果就开始第二次转码。用全局“上一次结果”时，很容易把第二次输出当成第一次输出。每次 `json_to_msgpack` 都返回自己的输出 id、精确长度和错误，保留两个结果对象就能分别读取两次操作。
输出：

blocks.code:
都成功: true
输出各自独立: true
第一个结果仍有效: true

blocks.text: 三行结果都是 `true`。第二次调用没有覆盖第一个结果。`finally` 分别释放成功输出、两个输入分配和两个元数据对象。

sections.id: 拒绝尾随第二个文档-避免静默丢数据
sections.heading: 拒绝尾随第二个文档，避免静默丢数据

blocks.text: 导出拼接出错时，一个缓冲里可能出现两个 JSON 文档。只读取第一个会看起来成功，却丢掉后面的数据。`json_to_msgpack` 要求输入是一个完整文档；尾随非空白字节会得到失败结果，输入分配仍由调用者拥有。
输出：

blocks.code:
输出分配: 0 字节数: 0
拒绝第二个文档: true
输入仍归调用方: true

blocks.text: 输出分配和长度都是 0，后面两个判断都是 `true`。失败没有留下输出块；调用者仍须释放输入和失败结果的元数据。

sections.heading: 只解码收到的 MessagePack 字节

blocks.text: 收到的五字节消息可能占用八字节的暂存区。如果把容量当成文档长度，解码器会把填充字节也读进去，让有效消息变成尾随字节错误。把收到的精确字节数传给 `msgpack_to_json`，并且只读取结果的 `result.len` 字节。
输出：

blocks.code:
文档: {"ok":true}
输入字节: 5 容量: 8

blocks.text: 输出 `文档: {"ok":true}` 和 `输入字节: 5 容量: 8`。文档长度不同于取整容量，转码只消费传入的精确文档字节。

默认初始化器导入为 `init`。`init({ module_or_path })` 接受请求字符串、`Request`、`URL`、`Response`、`BufferSource`、预编译 `WebAssembly.Module`，也接受这些输入的 Promise。省略参数时使用包内 `wasm_provider_bg.wasm` 网址。请求字符串、请求和网址走 `fetch`；字节和模块直接实例化。Node 示例通过包入口定位相邻资源并传入字节。加载失败时 Promise 拒绝。
`initSync({ module })` 接受字节或预编译 `WebAssembly.Module`，不发起网络获取，`module` 必填。已初始化时，两个入口都返回已发布导出。位置参数形式仍然接受，但会输出弃用警告；使用对象形式即可。
`InitOutput.memory` 是原生 `WebAssembly.Memory`。其余函数属于生成的原始 ABI：特别是转码函数返回数字元数据指针，释放函数返回数字布尔值。应用应使用具名导入的包装函数，得到 `ConversionResult` 和布尔值。不要把字节区 id 当成元数据指针。

rows: 请求的字节数，使用非负的无符号三十二位整数；容量向上取整为八的倍数。零长度分配成功后也拥有必须释放的 id。
同一已初始化模块中，来自 `alloc_bytes` 或成功 `ConversionResult.id` 的活动 id。零是保留哨兵，不是分配。不能传入字节指针。
实际写入输入的文档字节数，不超过 `byte_len_of(id)`。不能使用取整容量。
可选的模块来源，取值见上文。省略参数时默认使用包内 WASM 网址；提供字节时无需网络获取。
必填的字节或预编译模块。没有默认值，不接受需要网络获取的来源。

blocks.text: Rust 使用 `Vec<u64>` 管理同一个字节暂存区。分配 id 保持稳定，活动期间不会被复用。字节指针在对应 id 释放前保持有效。任何可能分配或增长内存的调用后，都应从当前 `memory.buffer` 重新创建视图。
`alloc_bytes` 在内存或 id 空间耗尽时返回 `0`。未知和已释放 id 的 `ptr_of`、`byte_len_of` 返回 `0`，`dealloc_bytes` 返回 `false`。活动的零长度分配容量同样为零，不能只凭容量判断是否仍然活动。

两个转码器都是同步的，只收发字节。成功返回 `{ id: nonzero, len: exactBytes, error: '' }`；失败返回 `{ id: 0, len: 0, error: reason }`。每次调用持有独立元数据。输入 id 和成功输出 id 都归调用者，用 `dealloc_bytes` 分别释放。每个返回的元数据对象，包括失败结果，还须另行调用 `free()` 或 `[Symbol.dispose]()`。释放元数据前读取所需字段；之后不要再读取或释放该元数据。释放元数据不会释放字节区，释放字节区也不会释放元数据。

转码拒绝未知 id、超过容量的长度、空文档、非法数据和尾随第二个文档。JSON 允许尾随空白，MessagePack 必须精确消费输入长度。失败没有留下输出块，调用者的输入分配和字节保持不变。JSON 读取器直接写入 MessagePack 输出，不先创建 `serde_json::Value` 树；对象的 map key 保持字符串。JSON 对象直接按 map 序列化，不依赖 struct-map 配置。
JSON 往返保真限于 JSON 数据模型及可表示数值。任意 MessagePack 的 bin/ext、非 JSON map key 和超范围整数不保证可逆，可能被改写或拒绝。

失败转码把文本放在本次 `error` 属性中，不使用全局错误槽。id 非法或长度超容量返回 `unknown allocation id or length past capacity`；输出分配耗尽返回 `arena exhausted`。解析错误分别以 `json to msgpack failed:` 或 `msgpack to json failed:` 开头。读取输出前先检查 `id`，保留原始错误文本用于诊断，最后释放失败元数据和输入。
原生 `WebAssembly.CompileError`、`WebAssembly.LinkError`、`WebAssembly.RuntimeError` 原样透传，保持类型、身份和堆栈，不附包级 `source` 或 `code`。它们与正常转码的失败返回值不同。本包没有自有错误码。

`@migaia/wasm` 负责 arena 和转码；`@migaia/store-wasm` 负责字段分配、数值视图与字段生命周期，不复制暂存区或转码状态机。字段 owner 通过 `ensureWasm()` 复用同一个初始化 Promise，显式 dispose 时释放自己的分配；构造失败时先回滚已创建资源，再保留原始错误。record 字段只接受 number，并使用当前 `memory.buffer` 上的 `DataView`。它的 `FinalizationRegistry` 只是兜底，不替代显式释放。

中文

`@migaia/wasm` provides aligned WASM byte storage and synchronous JSON–MessagePack conversion, with explicit ownership instead of passing JavaScript object graphs across the WASM boundary. MessagePack is a binary data format.

items: A numeric view throws `RangeError`. A byte allocator supplied an offset that was not aligned for `Float64Array` or `BigInt64Array`.
A reading disappears after a large allocation. A typed-array view was cached across memory growth and now points to a detached buffer.
The second export overwrites the first result. Output metadata was held in a shared last-result slot rather than attached to each operation.
An archive looks valid but loses its tail. Parsing accepted the first document without checking that all non-whitespace input was consumed.
A background upload changes after cleanup. The queue retained a view into freed WASM memory rather than a JavaScript-owned copy.

Numeric views need no separate alignment layer. Rust stores arena blocks as `Vec<u64>`, aligning addresses and rounding capacity to eight bytes; the numeric readings example constructs a `Float64Array` directly.
Interleaved conversions keep their own results. Each call returns its own output ID, exact length and error; the interleaving example retains two results before reading either.

A broken concatenation fails explicitly. The converters enforce one document rather than silently discarding a second; the trailing document example returns zero output with an operation-specific failure.

The boundary carries bytes throughout. The JSON reader writes directly to the MessagePack writer without building a `serde_json::Value` tree first; the interleaving example passes JSON bytes to the converter and retains each operation’s own output. This explains the mechanism, without claiming a speed advantage over native JSON operations.

The numeric view above throws `RangeError` because its offset is misaligned. Even with alignment fixed, memory growth requires fresh views. The module uses Rust `Vec<u64>` for alignment and stable IDs for live allocations; the first release returns true and a repeated release returns false.

blocks.text: The module includes the generated ES module and `.wasm` asset. In a browser with asset loading configured, `await init()` loads that bundled asset. Node hosts should pass bytes or a precompiled `WebAssembly.Module`, as above.

rows: Loads the module asynchronously and returns shared memory.
Initializes synchronously from bytes or a compiled module.
Owns an aligned, zeroed byte allocation.
Releases an input or successful output arena allocation.
Converts a complete JSON document to MessagePack.
Converts exact-length MessagePack bytes to JSON.

blocks.text: An arena is the module's byte store. `alloc_bytes(byte_len)` returns a stable nonzero allocation ID, or `0` on memory or identifier exhaustion. `ptr_of(id)` returns its byte offset; `byte_len_of(id)` returns capacity rounded up to eight bytes. Unknown or released IDs return `0` from both queries. `dealloc_bytes(id)` returns whether it removed a live block. Every successful allocation, including a zero-length allocation, needs explicit release.

`json_to_msgpack(id, len)` and `msgpack_to_json(id, len)` return a separate `ConversionResult` for each call. On success it holds a new output `id`, exact output `len` and empty `error`. On failure `id` and `len` are zero and `error` explains this operation's failure. Conversion never releases the input. Release input and successful output IDs with `dealloc_bytes`; separately call `result.free()` for metadata on both success and failure. `free()` does not release the output arena block.

The converters consume one complete document. JSON permits trailing whitespace; MessagePack must consume exactly the supplied length. Use the exact payload length, never rounded capacity. JSON object keys remain strings. JSON objects serialize directly as maps, independently of struct-map configuration. Roundtrip preservation is limited to the JSON data model and representable numbers; arbitrary MessagePack bin/ext values, non-JSON map keys and integers outside JSON's numeric range may change or be rejected.

Pointers stay stable until release, but memory growth replaces `memory.buffer`. Construct each view from the current buffer immediately before use. `.slice()` creates a JavaScript-owned copy that survives arena release. A zero-copy view requires its allocation to stay live until the last read. `@migaia/store-wasm` adds field ownership and a `FinalizationRegistry` fallback; it does not replace deterministic disposal or duplicate this arena.

The first completed initialization publishes the module exports. Concurrent calls and named wrappers use that same memory and arena; concurrent instantiation may still happen, and Promise identity or a single compilation is not guaranteed. Native `WebAssembly.CompileError`, `LinkError` and `RuntimeError` cross unchanged, without module `source` or `code`. Conversion failures are returned values rather than those native exceptions.

sections.heading: Share one arena when two features start together

blocks.text: Two features can initialize the module at the same time. Publishing the last instance would make one feature hold memory that the named wrappers no longer use. The initializer keeps the first completed exports, and every completed call returns that object. This does not promise one compilation or identical Promises.
Output:

blocks.code:
same exports: true
same allocation: true

blocks.text: Prints `same exports: true` and `same allocation: true`. Both initialization results and the named allocator address the same published arena.

sections.heading: Store numeric readings without guessing alignment

blocks.text: A byte offset that works for a byte array may throw RangeError when reused for Float64Array. Hand-written allocators must align the address and round capacity separately. alloc_bytes does both: a request for 9 bytes owns 16 zeroed bytes at an eight-byte-aligned address.
Output:

blocks.code:
capacity: 16
alignment remainder: 0
readings: 21.5 23

blocks.text: Prints capacity 16, alignment remainder 0 and readings 21.5 23. The rounded allocation can hold two Float64 values, and the pointer satisfies the native typed-array alignment requirement.

sections.heading: Read the same allocation after memory grows

blocks.text: A cached typed-array view can become detached after another allocation grows WebAssembly memory. A stable pointer does not keep its old ArrayBuffer alive. Keep the arena ID, query ptr_of, and create the view from the current memory.buffer immediately before reading.
Output:

blocks.code:
same offset: true
old view bytes: 0
current reading: 42

blocks.text: Prints `same offset: true`, `old view bytes: 0` and `current reading: 42`. The live arena allocation stays at its offset while memory growth detaches the old non-shared buffer.

sections.heading: Keep a JavaScript copy after releasing WASM bytes

blocks.text: An upload queue may outlive the conversion that produced its bytes. Keeping a view into a released arena block lets later allocations overwrite queued data. Copy the bytes before dealloc_bytes. A second release returns false and never frees a different live block.
Output:

blocks.code:
release: true false
copy: 1,2,3
released queries: 0 0

blocks.text: Prints `release: true false`, `copy: 1,2,3` and `released queries: 0 0`. The JavaScript copy survives; the released ID is no longer readable through the arena queries.

sections.heading: Retain two conversions without a shared last-result slot

blocks.text: A batch exporter may start another conversion before reading the first result. A global last-result slot makes the first output easy to confuse with the second. Each json_to_msgpack call returns its own output ID, exact length and error, so retaining both result objects keeps both operations distinct.
Output:

blocks.code:
both succeeded: true
separate outputs: true
first result retained: true

blocks.text: All three lines end in true. The second call leaves the first result intact. The finally block releases successful output IDs, both input IDs and both metadata objects independently.

sections.heading: Reject a second document instead of silently dropping it

blocks.text: A concatenated export can contain two JSON documents by mistake. Parsing only the first would report success while losing the second. json_to_msgpack requires one complete document and reports a failed result for trailing non-whitespace bytes; the input remains owned by the caller.
Output:

blocks.code:
output allocation: 0 bytes: 0
second document rejected: true
input still owned: true

blocks.text: Prints output allocation 0 and length 0, followed by two true values. No failed output allocation survives; the caller still frees the input and the failure metadata.

sections.heading: Decode only the received MessagePack bytes

blocks.text: A five-byte message can occupy an eight-byte arena block. Passing capacity as document length feeds padding to the decoder and turns valid input into a trailing-bytes failure. Pass the received byte length to msgpack_to_json and read exactly result.len bytes from its output.
Output:

blocks.code:
document: {"ok":true}
input bytes: 5 capacity: 8

blocks.text: Prints `document: {"ok":true}` and `input bytes: 5 capacity: 8`. Document length and rounded arena capacity are different, and the conversion uses only the supplied document bytes.

Import the default initializer as `init`. `init({ module_or_path })` accepts a request string, `Request`, `URL`, `Response`, `BufferSource` or precompiled `WebAssembly.Module`, including a Promise of that input. Omitting the argument selects the packaged `wasm_provider_bg.wasm` URL. Request strings, requests and URLs use `fetch`; byte and module inputs instantiate directly. The Node examples read the resource beside the resolved module entry and pass its bytes. Loading failures reject the Promise.

`initSync({ module })` accepts bytes or a precompiled `WebAssembly.Module` and never fetches. `module` is required. Both initializers return the already published exports when initialized. The positional forms remain accepted but emit a deprecation warning; use the object forms.

`InitOutput.memory` is native `WebAssembly.Memory`. Its other functions are the raw generated ABI: notably, its conversion functions return numeric metadata pointers and its release function returns a numeric boolean. Application code should use the named imported wrappers to receive `ConversionResult` and boolean results. Do not pass an arena ID as a raw metadata pointer.

rows: Requested byte count, a nonnegative unsigned 32-bit integer. Capacity rounds upward to a multiple of eight. Zero-length allocations still return an owned ID on success.
A live ID returned by `alloc_bytes` or a successful `ConversionResult.id` in this initialized module. Zero is reserved, not an allocation. Never substitute a pointer.
Exact count of document bytes written to the input, no greater than `byte_len_of(id)`. It is not rounded capacity.
Optional module source described above. The omitted argument defaults to the bundled WASM URL; supplied bytes work without network fetching.
Required bytes or precompiled module. No network-capable source and no default.

blocks.text: Rust owns one arena backed by `Vec<u64>`. The allocation ID remains stable and is not reused while live. A pointer remains valid until its ID is released. A view must be recreated from the current `memory.buffer` after any call that may allocate or grow memory.

`alloc_bytes` returns `0` on memory or identifier exhaustion. Unknown and released IDs return `0` from `ptr_of` and `byte_len_of`; `dealloc_bytes` returns `false`. A live zero-length allocation also has capacity zero, so capacity alone does not identify a live allocation.

Both converters are synchronous and byte-in/byte-out. Success returns `{ id: nonzero, len: exactBytes, error: '' }`; failure returns `{ id: 0, len: 0, error: reason }`. Each call has independent metadata. Both the input ID and successful output ID belong to the caller. Release each with `dealloc_bytes`. Every returned metadata object, including a failure, separately needs `free()` or `[Symbol.dispose]()`. Read required fields before releasing metadata; never read or free that metadata again. Releasing metadata does not release arena bytes, and releasing arena bytes does not release metadata.

Conversion rejects unknown IDs, lengths beyond capacity, empty documents, malformed data and a trailing second document. JSON allows trailing whitespace. MessagePack must consume exactly the supplied length. Failure leaves no output block and preserves the caller's input allocation and bytes. The JSON reader transcodes directly to the MessagePack writer without an intermediate `serde_json::Value` tree; map keys remain strings. JSON objects serialize directly as maps, independently of struct-map configuration.

JSON roundtrips cover the JSON data model and representable numbers. Arbitrary MessagePack bin/ext values, non-JSON map keys and out-of-range integers are not guaranteed reversible; they may be rewritten or rejected.

A failed conversion carries text in its own `error` property, not a global error slot. Invalid IDs and oversized lengths return `unknown allocation id or length past capacity`; output allocation exhaustion returns `arena exhausted`. Parsing errors begin with `json to msgpack failed:` or `msgpack to json failed:`. Check `id` before reading an output, retain the exact error for diagnostics, and always free failure metadata and the input.

Native `WebAssembly.CompileError`, `WebAssembly.LinkError` and `WebAssembly.RuntimeError` pass through unchanged, retaining their type, identity and stack without module `source` or `code`. They are separate from a normal conversion failure result. The module defines no custom error codes.

`@migaia/wasm` owns arena storage and transcoding. `@migaia/store-wasm` owns field allocations, numeric views and field lifetimes; it does not copy the arena or conversion state machine. Its field owner reuses one initialization Promise through `ensureWasm()`, releases allocations on explicit disposal, and rolls back already-created resources before surfacing a construction failure with the original error preserved. Record fields accept numbers and use `DataView` over the current `memory.buffer`. Its `FinalizationRegistry` is a fallback, not a replacement for explicit disposal.
